*Early Life* Raymond III was born around 1140 in the Crusader State of Tripoli. He was the son of Raymond II Count of Tripoli and his wife Hodierna of Jerusalem. He inherited the county after his father death in 1152 when he was still a child. His mother acted as regent until he reached maturity. During his youth he was educated in the Latin Christian tradition and learned the arts of war and diplomacy. He married Eschiva of Bures which gave him a claim to the Principality of Galilee and the city of Tiberias. This marriage strengthened his ties to the nobility of Jerusalem and expanded his influence beyond Tripoli.

*Reign and Politics* Raymond III assumed full rule in the mid 1150s and quickly became a major player in the politics of the Outremer. He pursued an independent foreign policy that sometimes clashed with the King of Jerusalem. He negotiated treaties with the Byzantine Empire seeking military aid and trade advantages. He also engaged in frequent skirmishes with Muslim neighbours especially the forces of Nur ad-Din and later Saladin. Raymond was known for his shifting alliances he would support the King when it suited his interests and oppose him when he felt his own authority threatened. He played a role in the succession disputes after the death of Baldwin IV and backed the claim of Sibylla against that of Isabella. His rivalry with Guy of Lusignan grew after Guy married Sibylla and became king. Raymond refused to attend Guy coronation and withheld military support during the early years of Guy reign. This tension culminated in the lead up to the Battle of Hattin where Raymond stayed in Tripoli rather than join the royal army. His decision was motivated by a desire to protect his own lands and to pressure Guy into recognizing his claims.

*Death and Legacy* After the disastrous defeat at Hattin in July 1187 Raymond III remained in Tripoli while the Crusader army was destroyed. He attempted to negotiate with Saladin for the safety of his county and family. Saladin laid siege to Tripoli later that year and the city held out for several months. Raymond died in September 1187 shortly before the fall of Tripoli to Muslim forces. His death marked the end of an era of relatively autonomous Crusader rule in the north. He was remembered as a capable lord who balanced local interests with the broader politics of the Latin East. His descendants continued to hold titles in the region for a generation though the political landscape had shifted dramatically after the loss of Jerusalem. Historians view Raymond III as a figure who embodied the complexities of Crusader nobility his actions illustrate the frequent tension between personal ambition and collective defence of the Frankish states.
